positioning: Tourette syndrome is a large, under-diagnosed pediatric neuro-psychiatric market where the only approved drugs are decades-old antipsychotics — and ecopipam is the first novel mechanism, and first non-antipsychotic, to reach the FDA in more than a decade.

sections.title: The market today
sections.body: About 174,000 US children are diagnosed with Tourette syndrome (~1 in 333, 0.3%), but roughly half of all cases go undiagnosed — implying ~1 in 162 children (0.6%) are truly affected. It is a large, under-identified pediatric population managed today with decades-old generic antipsychotics and off-label alpha-2 agonists.

sections.title: The patient journey
sections.body: Families consult about four different clinicians over years before diagnosis; care concentrates in pediatric neurology and child psychiatry and is mediated by caregivers and schools. The bottleneck is diagnosis and specialist access — not treatment capacity.

sections.title: Who treats it — and how
sections.body: Only three drugs are FDA-approved for tics (haloperidol, pimozide, aripiprazole — all D2 antipsychotics with EPS and metabolic liabilities), while real-world first-line care leans on behavioral therapy (CBIT) and off-label generic alpha-2 agonists. Everything effective today is either old, off-label, or hard to access.

sections.title: The economic opportunity
sections.body: Third-party analysts size the TS treatment market at roughly $2.0–2.7B, a base that is largely generic today; a differentiated, on-label branded entrant is the value-creation opportunity, with sell-side peak-sales estimates for ecopipam of up to ~$1B. (External estimates — this tool does not model revenue.)

sections.title: What's missing — why it's worth pursuing
sections.body: The guideline ladder pushes antipsychotics down for tolerability, first-line CBIT is throttled by a therapist shortage, and no new mechanism has arrived in over a decade — leaving experts, patients, and caregivers with options that are effective-but-toxic or effective-but-inaccessible. A weight-neutral, non-antipsychotic mechanism with positive Phase 3 data is the first credible answer to that gap.

one_liner: A large, under-served pediatric market with no modern mechanism — and a first-in-class, non-antipsychotic asset with positive Phase 3 data positioned to define it.
